units.name: 31 Solo Dining
units.passage: For many years, people who ate by themselves at restaurants were often seen as lonely or cut off from society. These days, however, that picture is changing quickly. According to recent figures, solo diners in the UK have more than doubled over just two years, and tables for one are now the fastest-growing type of restaurant booking there. As this trend spreads, the negative image attached to eating alone is fading. Some people even think that a person dining alone in public looks confident and successful, like someone rewarding themselves for their hard work. After the BBC ran a story on this topic, one reader described a personal change of heart. Only a few years before, the idea of going out to eat alone had seemed gloomy to this reader, and anyone seen doing it looked sad. Today, this same person often eats out alone and sometimes even likes it better than eating with friends. In this reader's view, people who dine alone are not really alone anymore. Some go further and say that a meal by yourself is like a date with someone you love.

units.name: 32 Galaxies
units.passage: Until the 1900s, scientists who studied the sky knew surprisingly little about the galaxy we live in. They had recorded hundreds of stars in the Milky Way, and they had also spotted many dim, cloudy patches of light, which they named nebulae. A number of these patches were clouds of gas connected to stars being born or dying. Others, however, were different. Their spiral or oval forms seemed too neat and orderly to be simple clouds. In 1920, two well-known astronomers held a famous debate about where these strange nebulae came from. Harlow Shapley claimed that everything visible in the sky belonged to the Milky Way. Heber Curtis, on the other hand, suggested that some nebulae were whole galaxies lying far outside ours. Many expected that the question would remain open for decades. Yet only a few years later, Edwin Hubble, working with the strongest telescope of his day, proved that certain nebulae were indeed independent galaxies. All at once, the universe became an enormous canvas, and people learned that other galaxies really did exist beyond our own.

units.name: 33 Cognitive Bias
units.passage: The Actor-Observer Bias describes a common pattern in how we explain behavior. When we judge other people, we tend to blame their actions on internal causes, such as their character. When we judge ourselves, however, we usually point to external causes. Imagine a student with low grades who meets a school advisor to talk about the problem. The student arrives late for the meeting. When the advisor asks why the grades are so poor, the student lists outside factors: too many classes, troubles at home, and a lot of stress. In other words, the student blames the situation and overlooks any personal responsibility. The advisor nods as if agreeing, but secretly thinks differently. In the advisor's mind, the poor results come from the student's personality, such as laziness or a lack of focus, and the possible effect of the circumstances is given too little weight. In truth, both kinds of causes are probably involved in this case.

units.name: 34 Shrinkflation
units.passage: The word shrinkflation was formed by joining two words, shrink and inflation. It describes a situation in which a company makes its products smaller but does not lower the price. Businesses often turn to this method when the cost of producing goods goes up. If materials or workers become more expensive, a company has to find some way to cut spending. One solution is to put less into each package, for example by lowering its weight, its volume, or the number of items inside. In this way, the company can protect the profit it earns on every sale. This strategy lets businesses keep or even raise their earnings while their prices still look attractive next to those of rival brands. Shrinkflation can also help a company hold on to its customers. When prices go up, shoppers may simply move to a cheaper brand. However, if a product becomes just a little smaller instead, buyers are less likely to leave, so the company keeps both its customers and its profits.

units.name: 35 The Art of Passive Voice
units.passage: "Don't be afraid of the passive voice." This may sound like an overly simple tip, but it points to a useful job that the passive voice can do in writing. In fact, it lets a writer choose what to put in focus and what to leave in the background. Look at three ways to describe one event: "Pooh finished the honey" uses the active voice and names the actor; "The honey was finished by Pooh" is passive and still names the actor; and "The honey was finished" is passive with no actor at all. You might want the last version if the only thing that counts is that the honey is gone, not the fact that Pooh was the one who ate it. Only the passive voice gives you this choice. In the same way, a news report saying that "helicopters were sent to battle a fire" works well when the helicopters themselves are the key point, not the pilots who flew them. Readers don't have to be told that a man named Bob was at the controls of one of them.

units.name: 36 Optimistic Personality
units.passage: Becoming an optimistic person takes more than simply expecting good results in particular situations, which psychologists call "positive outcome expectancies." Of course, it helps to face a single event with a hopeful attitude, but real optimism reaches far beyond one-time moments. It means building hopeful beliefs that cover many parts of life, so that they can apply to all kinds of situations and difficulties, from school and work to friendships and health. In addition, for such beliefs to become a true part of someone's personality, they have to stay steady over time. A person who feels positive one day and hopeless the next cannot really be called optimistic. An optimistic disposition, then, means holding general positive beliefs that remain the same not only from day to day but also across weeks, months, and even many years. Such a lasting positive outlook is the base of an optimistic personality, and it shapes the way a person sees the world, filling it with hope.

units.name: 37 Store Design
units.passage: Walk into almost any big chain drugstore, and you will notice that the pharmacy counter sits at the very back. This layout is no accident. Because people must pass through the entire shop to reach it, they see many other goods along the way and may pick up a few extra items. However, the plan has a weak point, and stores need to deal with it so that it does not work against them. Customers who come for medicine usually have an urgent errand on their minds. They want to get their prescription and leave, so they rarely stop to look around while returning to the exit. To solve this problem, drugstores arrange their products for people facing both directions. Some displays, signs, and fixtures are set up to catch the eye of shoppers heading from the back toward the front door. In a way, the owners design two separate stores in a single space: one for people walking in and another for people walking out. They are willing to make this extra effort because the pharmacy is such a powerful tool for drawing customers through every part of the shop.

units.name: 38 Numeral 0
units.passage: In mathematics, the word for nothing is "zero." Interestingly, this word can be traced back to sunya, a Hindu term for "emptiness," because the concept of zero was first developed by mathematicians in India. The ancient Greeks and Romans, on the other hand, could not accept the idea at all. To them, it made no sense that nothing could be treated as a number. Since their number systems had no sign for zero, they were unable to use the handy "positional" method of writing numbers, in which the place of each digit decides its value. For instance, in 307, the 3 means three hundreds, the 0 shows that there are no tens, and the 7 means seven ones. Without this method, even simple multiplication with Roman numerals was terribly difficult. Hindu thinkers, in contrast, were already comfortable with emptiness thanks to Buddhist ideas, so using a symbol that meant nothing did not trouble them. Later, Arab scholars carried their way of writing numbers to Europe in the Middle Ages, which gave us what we now call "Arabic numerals." Along the way, sunya turned into the Arabic sifr, and this word lives on in English as both "zero" and "cipher."

units.name: 39 Sleep
units.passage: Scientists are now very excited about one question: what does the brain do while we sleep at night? According to Dr. Matthew Walker of UC Berkeley, a sleeping brain moves the things it learned during the day into parts of the brain where they can be kept more efficiently. Every stage of sleep has a special job in holding on to memories. Think about learning a foreign language. You must learn new words, remember new sounds through your ears, and train the muscles you use to pronounce each word correctly. The new words are put together by one particular area of the brain during the first hours of sleep, in a deep and dreamless stage called "slow-wave sleep." The motor skills needed for speaking are handled in stage 2 non-REM sleep, while memories of sounds are worked on throughout every stage. In addition, memories with strong feelings attached are dealt with during REM sleep, the stage linked to dreaming. In short, if you learn more during the day, you will need more sleep that night.

units.name: 40 Interesting Habitats
units.passage: Have you ever thought about how much wood is drifting across the sea? A surprisingly large amount of it is out there. Once a piece of driftwood floats away from the shore to begin a new life in the ocean, it will probably never come back to land. Still, getting lost at sea is not always the end of its journey. Actually, driftwood can keep floating for around 17 months, and during that time it offers things that are hard to find in the open ocean: food, shade, shelter from the waves, and a safe spot for laying eggs. Because of this, a log in the water turns into a kind of "floating reef" where many sea creatures can live. One example is the wingless water strider. This insect lives only in the ocean, and it lays its eggs on drifting wood. On top of that, more than 100 other kinds of invertebrates and about 130 kinds of fish are known to do well by using driftwood.

units.name: 41 Microbes
units.passage: Microorganisms, or microbes, like bacteria and viruses, obviously cannot think, since they have no brains. They have no idea what they are doing to you, in the same way that you never think twice about the countless microbes you kill while taking a shower. Your health becomes important to them in only one case: when they kill you too effectively. If they finish you off before they have had a chance to move on to new hosts, they might disappear along with you. In fact, this does happen from time to time. As the writer Jared Diamond points out, history has many examples of diseases that once spread terrible epidemics and then vanished as strangely as they had appeared. One of them is the English sweating sickness. This dangerous illness lasted only from 1485 to 1552, and it killed tens of thousands of people before it burned itself out. Being too efficient, then, is bad news for any organism that causes infection.

units.passage: Preparations for the Columbian Expo in Chicago were moving along well, but Daniel Burnham, the architect who led the project, was far from happy. He wanted the fair to be so impressive that it would easily outshine the Paris Exposition, which had just ended. The problem was that Chicago had nothing to match the wonderful tower Gustave Eiffel had designed for Paris, which had thrilled everyone who saw it. With this goal in mind, Burnham asked for an idea that would be truly great. People offered plans for all kinds of huge towers. One was to be two miles tall, and another was to be built out of logs. Burnham rejected every one of them, because he wanted something totally new. Then an engineer from Pittsburgh came up with a plan. He would create a gigantic wheel that could carry riders hundreds of feet up into the air. Completed in less than six months, the amazingly huge wheel was able to hold over two thousand people at once. Since then, the Ferris wheel has been part of our lives.

units.name: 43 Strategies of Plants
units.passage: Plants cannot walk, but they still need to send their young to places where they can take root and carry their genes forward. To do this, many of them catch a ride on animals. Wild strawberries are a good example. While the seeds inside are immature and not ready to sprout, the fruit around them stays green, hard, and sour. Once the seeds are fully developed, however, the berries become red, soft, and sweet. This shift in color works like a sign that draws birds. The birds eat the ripe berries, fly away, and later drop the seeds somewhere else. Of course, strawberry plants never planned to invite birds only at the right moment. Rather, they developed this pattern through natural selection. Plants whose young berries were greener and more sour lost fewer seeds to birds that ate the fruit too early. At the same time, plants whose ripe berries were redder and sweeter had more birds carrying their mature seeds away. Over many generations, these useful traits became common.

units.name: 44 Language Acquisition
units.passage: Humans learn to speak in a way that resembles something seen in songbirds. Young birds of species that must learn their songs go through a stage called subsong, during which they try out different sounds. Surprisingly, this stage starts at the expected time even when a bird cannot hear. Human babies have a similar stage called babbling. By trying sounds again and again and correcting their mistakes, they gradually gain the ability to make the consonants used in their native language. Just like the birds, deaf babies start and stop babbling at the usual age. This gives us good reason to think that the rhythms we use to put words and sentences together, as well as grammar rules such as sorting words into nouns, verbs, adverbs, and adjectives, are built into the human mind from birth. Noam Chomsky made this argument most convincingly. His view helps explain why children pick up speech so easily, while they struggle with tasks that are much simpler by nature, such as adding and subtracting numbers.

units.name: 45 Coffee Machine Sounds
units.passage: Back in the 1920s, the psychologist Ivan Pavlov noticed something famous: his dogs began to drool when they heard a bell that told them food was coming. Coffee machines work in a similar way on our minds. The grinding, bubbling, sputtering, and hissing they make give us clues about how the drink will taste. An experienced barista can even judge how hot the milk is just by listening to the high sounds it makes while it foams. A researcher named Klemens Knöferle found that when a coffee machine's sounds were changed, people's opinions about the taste of the coffee changed too. When the high-pitched noises were made louder, people gave the coffee lower scores for taste. When those noises were turned down, the scores rose. For this reason, many companies today are trying to build machines that make just the right sounds so that customers enjoy their coffee more.

units.name: 46 Enlightenment
units.passage: Being informed means simply knowing that something is true. Being enlightened goes further. It means also understanding what that fact is really about: why it is true, how it is linked to other facts, and in which ways it is similar to or different from them. We know this difference well as the gap between remembering something and knowing how to explain it. Suppose you can recall the words of a writer. Then you have gained something from his book. If his words are true, you have also picked up some knowledge of the world. However, whether the fact you have gained concerns the book or the world, it is only information if you have used nothing but your memory. Put another way, you have not reached enlightenment. You become enlightened only when you understand not just what a writer says but also its meaning and the reason he says it.

units.name: 47 Context
units.passage: How we act in a given situation depends greatly on our surroundings. We speak quietly in hospitals, feel nervous at police stations, grow sad at graveyards, and get excited at parties. A large number of the settings that influence us most strongly are learned when we are young. For example, what our eyes are exposed to early in life may actually shape how we see things later. Researchers compared Euro-Canadians who grew up in cities full of buildings with right angles and Cree Indians who were raised around tents with many different shapes and angles. The study suggested that early visual surroundings can have long-lasting effects. As adults, the Euro-Canadians recognized right angles more easily than lines in other directions. However, they seemed less skilled than the Cree at seeing lines at other angles. Since the Cree have a different mental picture of the world from the start, they may be able to notice a wider range of visual signals.

units.name: 48 Research Validity
units.passage: A great deal of psychological research uses students, mostly undergraduates, as its subjects. Because of this, the research may give a slightly twisted picture of how much people depend on reasoning rather than feelings when they make everyday choices. The reason is that undergraduates have strong thinking skills, which is a key factor, and they tend to use these skills more than other people do. Why, then, do psychologists accept such possible biases? A cynical answer is that it is simply convenient: most researchers can easily reach large numbers of students on campus. Researchers also believe that what they learn from students can be applied to other groups, since student life has much in common with what adults call real life. For instance, college students must work out precisely what others expect from them, how much effort meeting those demands will require, and how to finish the work well and quickly, just as people do when they start a new and harder job.

units.name: 49 Twinkling Stars
units.passage: When we look up at the night sky, the moving air of our atmosphere makes every image less sharp. Even on a perfectly clear night, stars seem to twinkle and flicker. Stars low near the horizon flicker more than stars right above our heads, because their light must travel through more moving air before it reaches us. There is a second problem as well. Light bends slightly as it passes the edge of a lens, and this effect, called diffraction, means that the size of a telescope's lens sets a fixed limit on how tightly starlight can be focused. For this reason, astronomers choose the places for their telescopes very carefully. On Earth, they put them on high mountains, where the air is thin, or close to the coast, where the air flows smoothly. However, the ideal place for sharp pictures is space itself, since it has no atmosphere at all. That is why the Hubble Space Telescope, which travels around the Earth, has taken the deepest pictures of the universe ever made.

units.name: 50 Consumer Loyalty
units.passage: Why do many people use only a few websites when they shop online for cheaper versions of the same product? One possible answer comes from the human capital model, suggested by Becker in 1993. According to this model, people gain knowledge mainly by learning through doing. As time passes and experience builds up, we develop the abilities that help us survive and succeed in our society. When we try something new, it usually takes a lot of effort. With repeated practice, however, actions that once felt hard and tiring gradually get easier, and in the end they turn into habits. Online shopping works the same way. A website that shoppers have already used before is more helpful to them because it reduces the amount of mental energy they need. Since a familiar site is so easy to use, shoppers end up becoming loyal to that single site. This is why many consumers do not compare prices across different online stores, even though doing so would take very little work.

units.name: 51 Adults vs. Infants
units.passage: As adults, when we focus on one thing, we become more open to information about it, while the rest of our brain is held back. This works like a spotlight. We ignore the many distractions around us and concentrate on a single thing at a time. Babies, however, are very poor at this, because their awareness is less like a spotlight and more like a lantern. They take in everything that is happening around them at once. What babies cannot do well is inhibition, which means they are poor at blocking things out and easily distracted. Still, there are some situations in which adults process information much like babies do. One example is visiting an unfamiliar city for the first time. In such moments, we feel as though our awareness has grown wider. As a result, we may remember three days in Bangkok more vividly than all the months we spend at home, where we walk, talk, work, and attend meetings almost like robots.

items.q:

units.name: 52 Reasoning
units.passage: For a long time, many scientists and thinkers believed that doing science meant looking for evidence that supports your hypothesis. Suppose you wanted to show that every swan is white. You would observe as many white swans as possible. If each swan you checked turned out to be white, it seemed sensible to accept your hypothesis as true. This kind of reasoning moves from the statement "Every swan I have observed is white" to the general claim "Every swan is white." Clearly, though, a swan you have never seen might be black. In fact, black swans live in Australia and can be found in many zoos across the world. Therefore, the conclusion does not logically follow from the evidence. This is an example of what is called the Problem of Induction. Even after you have examined thousands of swans and found only white ones, your conclusion could still be proven wrong. The only way to be completely sure that all swans are white is to check every single swan in existence. If even one black swan is found, your conclusion falls apart.

units.name: 53 Nature’s Clues
units.passage: Nature is full of clues, and their beauty is something anyone can see without studying math. The mathematical stories that begin with these clues and work out the hidden rules behind them are also beautiful, but in another way: their beauty belongs to ideas, not to objects. Mathematics relates to nature in the same way that Sherlock Holmes relates to evidence. From nothing more than the end of a cigar, the famous detective in the stories could work out its owner's age, job, and how much money he had. His friend Dr. Watson, who did not notice such details as well, could only watch in puzzled wonder until Holmes explained his flawless chain of reasoning. In a similar way, mathematicians who are given data about how populations grow over time can figure out many basic principles of population change. Likewise, by studying six-sided snowflakes, they can work out how the atoms in ice crystals are arranged. In short, our universe speaks the language of mathematics.

units.name: 54 Food Science
units.passage: People often call cooking an art. In India, there is even a phrase, kai manam, meaning "hand flavor," for people who are born with a natural sense of taste. Such knowledge is believed to live in a cook's hands instead of the head, so it is hard to teach to anyone else. However, if we see traditional cooking purely as an art and ignore the methods and vocabulary of modern science and engineering, we may end up just following recipes without really understanding why they work. One useful way to become a better cook is to learn the basics of food science, such as how heat behaves and how water reacts chemically. Once you know what heat does to grains, vegetables, meat, eggs, and fats, and what physical and chemical changes happen at different temperatures, you will gain more skill and control in the kitchen.

units.name: 55 Frame
units.passage: In politics, the first step toward winning votes is often to shape how people see the current situation: as a gain or as a loss. Politicians who present today as a gain like to point out how much life has improved compared with earlier times. This message aims to build support for keeping things as they are, and it benefits the leaders who can take credit for the progress. Such a frame works best on voters who pay close attention to the past. In contrast, politicians who present today as a loss stress how much worse conditions have become than they used to be. The goal of this message is to create a desire for change, and it pushes voters toward the party that cannot be blamed for the decline. This second frame is most powerful with voters whose minds are fixed on the present and the future. In short, the same facts can lead people in very different directions, depending on whether they are described as progress or as damage.

units.name: 56 Deliberate Violation
units.passage: Sometimes people break rules and procedures on purpose. They may do so because they see no other way to finish their work, because they think their situation is a special exception, or because they bet that a small chance of failure will never happen to them. The problem is that rare events are not so rare on a large scale. If a risky action causes injury or death only once in a million cases, it can still kill hundreds of people every year in a world of 7 billion. Consider a case from aviation. A pilot once saw that the oil pressure gauges on each of his three engines showed low levels. He decided that the instruments must be broken, since the odds that the gauges were correct were only one in a million. His reasoning about the odds was right, but sadly, his flight turned out to be that single case. In 2012, about 9 million flights took off in the United States alone, so even odds of one in a million could mean around nine incidents in that year.

units.name: 57 Fan Work
units.passage: Racheline Maltese writes fan work, which means stories, novels, and other pieces built on characters and worlds taken from other people's professional creations. Writers like her usually share their work on the internet for free, simply because they enjoy it. They love the original stories, but they are not quiet consumers who only watch and read. Popular culture speaks to them, and they answer it using its own language. However, the authors whose works are borrowed hold very different opinions. Some welcome fan work, since it often spreads word about their books like free advertising. Others feel as though someone has stolen their characters. This raises difficult questions. Do characters belong to their creators or to the fans who adore them? Is art about inventing something completely new, or about reshaping materials that already exist? Whatever the answer is, fan work points to a cultural trend: readers want to take a creative part in the stories they love. This trend challenges much of what we believed about art and creativity.

units.name: 58 Brain Potential
units.passage: Learning how the brain responds to regular use and to curiosity can give us useful clues about how to learn better. Just as muscles become stronger when we use them more, the amygdala, a part of the brain, is believed to grow a kind of mental muscle. Research shows that when people use this region more often, they become more balanced both emotionally and intellectually. Instead of pulling back in fear when they meet something new, they respond to it with confidence. Curiosity plays an important role, too. It switches on parts of the hippocampus, which makes the experience of learning more enjoyable and helps us remember information for longer. In fact, the more curious you feel about a topic, the stronger your emotional reaction becomes. That emotion strengthens long-term memories, so you can hold on to new knowledge or skills. In other words, a brain that is used often and fed by curiosity is a brain that learns well.

units.name: 59 Behavior Change
units.passage: When we talk about the few people who behave badly, we may actually tempt others to copy them. So if we want to stop a certain behavior, we should do the opposite of exposing it. We should keep other people's bad actions out of sight and point to good results instead. Psychologist Bob Cialdini tested this idea at a national park in Arizona. Many visitors there took pieces of petrified wood, partly because the fossils could be sold or kept as souvenirs. To reduce the theft, he placed signs with different messages around the park. One sign said that many earlier visitors had taken petrified wood and had harmed the natural condition of the forest. Surprisingly, this message nearly doubled the number of people who took wood. Another set of signs simply asked visitors to leave the wood where it was so that the natural forest could be protected. Because these signs focused on the good that comes from leaving the wood, instead of on the actions of other visitors, they helped cut down on theft.

choices: 도난이 완전히 사라졌다.
방문객 수가 절반으로 줄었다.

report
increase
explain

items.q: 다음 문장의 [to leave]와 쓰임이 같은 것은? "Another set of signs simply asked visitors [to leave] the wood where it was."
choices: I want to leave early today.
My mom told me to clean my room.
He went to the store to buy milk.
I have no time to rest now.
To swim in the sea is fun.

the history of national parks in Arizona
how psychologists design park signs
focusing on positive outcomes rather than others' misbehavior to change behavior
why visitors collect souvenirs on trips

items.q: According to the passage, why did many visitors take pieces of petrified wood?
choices: Because park rangers encouraged them to.
Because the signs told them it was allowed.
Partly because the fossils could be sold or kept as souvenirs.
Because the wood was needed for campfires.
Because they wanted to protect the forest.

items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

items.q: 다음 중 글의 문장을 옮긴 것으로 어법상 틀린 것은?

units.name: 60 The Middle Ages
units.passage: As trade grew during the High Middle Ages, towns located along European seas and overland trade routes set up trade fairs. At these fairs, merchants from many regions gathered to pay off debts and arrange deals for the future. Over time, a few fairs became more successful than the others and turned into yearly events held in places such as Champagne, Ghent, Leipzig, and Winchester. The nobles who owned the land where the fairs took place were also involved, though in their own special way. They offered various services: courts to resolve arguments between traders, guards to protect merchants and their goods, clerks to handle documents, and buildings where people could meet. The fairs mattered not only for trading goods but also for spreading ideas. Because they drew people from many countries, thoughts and news from distant places were shared in countless conversations. Gradually, these fairs helped bring Europe's peasants and lords out of their isolation.

items.q: 글의 주제로 가장 알맞은 것은?
choices: the daily lives of European peasants
how nobles collected taxes from merchants
trade fairs of the Middle Ages and their roles
the decline of trade in medieval Europe
famous cities of modern Europe
items.exp: 중세 무역 박람회가 생겨난 배경, 귀족의 역할, 상품과 생각의 교류라는 역할을 설명하는 글이에요.

items.q: 글의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?

상인들은 박람회에서 빚을 갚고 앞으로의 거래를 준비했다.
일부 박람회는 샴페인, 겐트 등지의 연례 행사가 되었다.
박람회는 상품 거래에만 중요했고 생각의 교류와는 관련이 없었다.
박람회는 유럽 농민과 영주의 고립을 끝내는 데 도움을 주었다.
items.exp: 'mattered not only for trading goods but also for spreading ideas'라고 했으므로 ④는 틀려요.

분쟁을 해결하는 법정
상인과 물품을 지키는 경비병
서류를 처리하는 서기
사람들이 만날 수 있는 건물
items.exp: 귀족들은 법정, 경비병, 서기, 건물을 제공했다고 했고 돈을 빌려줬다는 내용은 없어요.

items.q: 지문의 resolve와 문맥상 의미가 가장 가까운 것은?
choices: start

record
forget
cause
items.exp: courts to resolve arguments는 다툼을 '해결하는' 법정이라는 뜻으로 settle과 같아요.

items.q: 다음 문장의 [where]와 쓰임이 같은 것은? "The nobles who owned the land [where] the fairs took place were also involved."

items.q: 글의 제목으로 가장 알맞은 것은?

Medieval Trade Fairs: Markets of Goods and Ideas

items.q: According to the passage, why were thoughts and news from distant places shared at the fairs?
choices: Because nobles ordered merchants to share news.
Because the fairs were held in universities.
Because merchants were forbidden to trade goods.
Because clerks printed newspapers at the fairs.
Because the fairs drew people from many countries.

items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

As trade (A) ___ in the High Middle Ages, fairs supported by local nobles became centers not only for business but also for the (B) ___ of ideas across Europe.
choices: (A) expanded — (B) exchange
(A) declined — (B) exchange
(A) expanded — (B) censorship

items.q: 밑줄 친 [in their own special way]가 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은? (The nobles who owned the land where the fairs took place were also involved, though in their own special way.)

guards to [protect] merchants and their goods
As trade [declined] during the High Middle Ages
thoughts and news from distant places were [shared]
